statement: A top-10 risk presentation to executive leadership should include timelines for risk eliminations.
explanation: Each top-10 risk is shown with its ranking, description, inherent and residual components, and an outlook (improving, worsening or status quo). Risks are mitigated rather than eliminated, so no elimination timeline is included.
originalText: timelines for risk eliminations.

statement: A top-10 risk presentation to executive leadership should include descriptions of the risks.
explanation: Each risk in the top-10 presentation is accompanied by a description, along with its ranking, inherent and residual components, and outlook.
originalText: descriptions of the risks.

statement: A top-10 risk presentation to executive leadership should include the inherent and residual elements of each risk.
explanation: For each risk the presentation shows the inherent likelihood, severity and rating and the corresponding residual components.
originalText: inherent and residual elements of each risk.

statement: A top-10 risk presentation to executive leadership should present the risks in a ranked order based on likelihood and severity.
explanation: Ranking by the magnitude of each risk, driven by its likelihood and severity, is a standard element of the top-10 presentation.
originalText: a ranked order based on likelihood and severity.

statement: Horizon scanning is one of the three options for aggregating qualitative risk data for reporting.
explanation: The three options are conversion and addition, categorization, and worst-case reporting. Horizon scanning is a forward-looking identification technique, not an aggregation method.
originalText: Horizon scanning
correction: Worst-case reporting is one of the three options for aggregating qualitative risk data for reporting.

statement: Conversion and addition is one of the three options for aggregating qualitative risk data for reporting.
explanation: Qualitative metrics can be converted to numeric scores and added together. The other two options are categorization and worst-case reporting.
originalText: Conversion and addition

statement: Categorization is one of the three options for aggregating qualitative risk data for reporting.
explanation: Categorization reports counts or proportions by colour or score band, for example red, amber and green.
originalText: Categorization

statement: Worst-case reporting is one of the three options for aggregating qualitative risk data for reporting.
explanation: Worst-case reporting is the most conservative option: the worst score in the group is the one reported.
originalText: Worst‑case reporting

statement: The asymmetry of operational risk event data is a challenge in non-financial risk reporting.
explanation: Operational loss data are heavily skewed, with many small events and a few very large ones, which makes averages and aggregate loss reporting difficult.
originalText: Asymmetry of operational risk event data

statement: When benchmarking operational losses across business units, losses should be reported in dollar terms rather than as percentages or basis points.
explanation: Business units differ in size, so benchmarking needs scale-free measures such as a percentage of gross income or budget, or basis points of capital, rather than raw dollar amounts.
originalText: When benchmarking across business units, losses should be reported in dollar terms rather than as percentages or basis points, because low percentages could mask high dollar losses.

statement: The central operational risk function should focus scarce resources on preventing and addressing major incidents rather than being distracted by daily volatility.
explanation: Resources should target the prevention of large incidents, not frequent insignificant events that cause day-to-day noise in the data.
originalText: The ORF should focus scarce resources on preventing and addressing major incidents rather than being distracted by daily volatility.

statement: The central operational risk function should regularly review small, frequent losses to spot potential control breaches or process flaws; if these losses are random and stable, their average cost can be included in the service price.
explanation: Small recurring losses can reveal control weaknesses. When they are random and stable, their average cost can simply be built into pricing.
originalText: The ORF should regularly review small, frequent losses to spot potential control breaches or process flaws; if these losses are random and stable, their average cost can be included in the service price.

statement: The central operational risk function can address the challenge of compiling qualitative risk data through conversion and addition, categorization, and worst-case reporting.
explanation: These are the three recognised methods for aggregating qualitative risk data into a report.
originalText: The ORF can address the challenge of compiling qualitative risk data through conversion and addition, categorization, and worst‑case reporting.

statement: Operational risk distributions do not lend themselves to using averages because there is minimal skewness in either the right or left tail.
explanation: Operational loss distributions are heavily skewed, which is one reason averages mislead. Minimal skewness would favour using the mean, not argue against it.
originalText: there is minimal skewness in either the right or left tail.
correction: Operational risk distributions do not lend themselves to using averages because the right tail is heavily skewed.

changes.from: there is minimal skewness in either the right or left tail
changes.to: the right tail is heavily skewed

statement: Operational risk distributions do not lend themselves to using averages because the distribution is asymmetric.
explanation: Asymmetry makes the mean unrepresentative of typical outcomes; averages work best for symmetric, bell-shaped distributions.
originalText: the distribution is asymmetric.

statement: Operational risk distributions do not lend themselves to using averages because the data may have significant variances.
explanation: A large variance means the mean hides how widely outcomes are dispersed.
originalText: the data may have significant variances.

statement: Operational risk distributions do not lend themselves to using averages because there may be a large quantity of outliers.
explanation: Outliers pull the mean away from typical values, and they are where most of the loss information lies.
originalText: there may be a large quantity of outliers.

statement: In a combined assurance approach, the central operational risk function (second line of defense) performs deep dives into specific types of risks.
explanation: The second line oversees first-line activities, performs sample control testing and carries out deep dives into specific risk types.
originalText: Deep dives into specific types of risks.

statement: In a combined assurance approach, the central operational risk function (second line of defense) performs internal audit reviews.
explanation: Periodic internal audit reviews are performed by the third line of defense, which provides independent assurance.
originalText: Internal audit reviews.

statement: In a combined assurance approach, the second line of defense oversees the activities performed by the third line.
explanation: The second line oversees the activities of the first line. The third line is independent and provides assurance over both of the other lines.
originalText: Oversight of the activities performed by the third line.
correction: In a combined assurance approach, the second line of defense oversees the activities performed by the first line.

statement: Risk appetite metrics are one of the three types of operational risk information that Pillar 3 requires banks to disclose.
explanation: The three required types are qualitative information on operational risk management, historical losses, and the business indicator and its subcomponents. Risk appetite metrics are internal reporting content, not a prescribed disclosure category.
originalText: Risk appetite metrics
correction: Historical losses are one of the three types of operational risk information that Pillar 3 requires banks to disclose.

statement: Qualitative information on operational risk management is one of the three types of operational risk information that Pillar 3 requires banks to disclose.
explanation: It covers governance, policies, systems and risk transfer arrangements. The other two types are historical losses and the business indicator with its subcomponents.
originalText: Qualitative information on operational risk management

statement: Historical losses are one of the three types of operational risk information that Pillar 3 requires banks to disclose.
explanation: Banks disclose 10 years of aggregate operational losses.
originalText: Historical losses

statement: The business indicator and its subcomponents are one of the three types of operational risk information that Pillar 3 requires banks to disclose.
explanation: The business indicator is the primary input to the operational risk capital calculation.
originalText: Business indicator and subcomponents

statement: Qualitative information on operational risk management is the Pillar 3 disclosure type that presents an entity's governance and risk management structures.
explanation: It describes the arrangements used to manage, mitigate or transfer operational risk, the structure of the risk management and control function, and the policies and procedures in place.
originalText: Qualitative information on operational risk management

statement: Historical losses are the Pillar 3 operational risk disclosure type that presents an entity's governance and risk management structures.
explanation: Historical losses are quantitative, consisting of 10 years of aggregate losses. Governance and risk management structures are described in the qualitative disclosure.
originalText: Historical losses

statement: The business indicator and its subcomponents are the Pillar 3 operational risk disclosure type that presents an entity's governance and risk management structures.
explanation: The business indicator and its subcomponents are quantitative inputs to the capital calculation. Governance and risk management structures are described in the qualitative disclosure.
originalText: Business indicators and subcomponents

statement: Basel operational risk disclosure requires historical loss data covering a minimum of 3 years of aggregate operational losses.
explanation: Pillar 3 requires 10 years of aggregate operational losses. A 3-year period applies only to some business indicator component data.
originalText: historical loss data covering a minimum of 3 years of aggregate operational losses.
correction: Basel operational risk disclosure requires historical loss data covering a minimum of 10 years of aggregate operational losses.

statement: Basel operational risk disclosure includes the arrangements the bank has in place to transfer operational risks.
explanation: Risk transfer arrangements form part of the required qualitative information on operational risk management.
originalText: arrangements the bank has in place to transfer operational risks.

statement: Basel operational risk disclosure includes information on the systems and data used to measure operational risk.
explanation: The systems and data used to measure operational risk are explicitly part of the qualitative disclosure.
originalText: information on systems and data used to measure operational risk.

statement: Basel operational risk disclosure includes narratives covering the key drivers of operational risk capital calculations.
explanation: Narratives on key drivers and significant changes accompany the quantitative data.
originalText: narratives covering key drivers of operational risk capital calculations.

statement: Functional is one of the criteria under which significant operational risk event triggers are categorized.
explanation: The four trigger criteria for notifying regulators are materiality, reputation, resilience and stability. Functional is not one of them.
originalText: functional.
correction: Resilience is one of the criteria under which significant operational risk event triggers are categorized.

statement: Stability is one of the criteria under which significant operational risk event triggers are categorized.
explanation: Stability covers events that could have serious consequences for the financial system.
originalText: stability.

statement: Materiality is one of the criteria under which significant operational risk event triggers are categorized.
explanation: Materiality covers events that are significant relative to a loss or materiality threshold.
originalText: materiality.

statement: Reputation is one of the criteria under which significant operational risk event triggers are categorized.
explanation: Reputation covers events that significantly affect the firm's reputation.
originalText: reputation.

statement: In the three lines of defense model, the first line, business line staff and management, owns and manages risk day to day, with decision-making authority and accountability, within the limits set by the risk appetite.
explanation: The first line holds the risk and acts as designated risk owner. Oversight is the second line, and independent assurance reporting to the board is the third line.
originalText: Business line staff and management own and manage risk day to day, with decision‑making authority and accountability, within the limits set by the risk appetite.

statement: Within an enterprise risk management framework, risk culture and corporate culture are independent and should be managed separately.
explanation: Risk culture cannot be separated from corporate culture, because both reflect the same shared values, beliefs and behaviors.
originalText: risk culture and corporate culture are independent and should be managed separately.
correction: Within an enterprise risk management framework, risk culture and corporate culture are inseparable.

changes.from: are independent and should be managed separately

statement: In an enterprise risk management framework, risk governance incorporates three to four standard lines of defense.
explanation: There are three internal lines of defense, and external audit is often regarded as a fourth.
originalText: risk governance incorporates three to four standard lines of defense.

statement: In an enterprise risk management framework, risk appetite may drive decisions that can lead to refining desired objectives.
explanation: Risk appetite and objectives interact: how much risk the firm will tolerate can feed back into the objectives it pursues.
originalText: risk appetite may drive decisions that can lead to refining desired objectives.

statement: In an enterprise risk management framework, reporting and monitoring are continuous because exposures to risk are constantly changing.
explanation: Exposures change over time, so risk must be monitored and reported on an ongoing basis.
originalText: reporting and monitoring are continuous due to constantly changing exposures to risk.

statement: An external auditor is often regarded as a fourth line of defense, sitting outside the three internal lines of defense.
explanation: The first line is business management, the second is risk oversight and the third is internal audit. External audit adds an extra layer of verification beyond these.
originalText: Fourth.

statement: In an enterprise risk management framework, governance sets the roles of the three lines of defense and reporting committees, culture reflects the behaviors and values around managing risk, and appetite defines the level of risk the firm is willing to tolerate.
explanation: Each of the three elements has a distinct function: governance assigns roles, culture shapes behavior, and appetite sets how much risk is tolerated.
originalText: Governance sets the roles of the three lines of defense and reporting committees, culture reflects the behaviors and values around managing risk, and appetite defines the level of risk the firm is willing to tolerate.

statement: In an enterprise risk management framework, governance defines the level of risk the firm is willing to tolerate, culture assigns the three lines of defense, and appetite reflects employee behaviors and values.
explanation: The functions are swapped. Governance assigns the roles of the lines of defense, culture reflects behaviors and values, and appetite defines the level of risk the firm will tolerate.
originalText: Governance defines the level of risk the firm is willing to tolerate, culture assigns the three lines of defense, and appetite reflects employee behaviors and values.

statement: Risk appetite in an enterprise risk management framework applies only to credit and market risk.
explanation: Risk appetite also covers other risks such as liquidity and operational risk.
originalText: Risk appetite applies only to credit and market risk, whereas governance and culture apply to operational risk.

statement: Risk culture is determined solely by the second line of defense, so governance and appetite do not influence it.
explanation: Risk culture is a firm-wide trait that involves executives, leadership and employees, and is not owned by one line. Governance and appetite both interact with it.

statement: Reverse stress testing applies mostly qualitative methods, targets immeasurable risks, and tries to identify the circumstances that might cause a firm to fail.
explanation: Reverse stress testing starts from a specific failure outcome and works backward to the circumstances that could produce it.
originalText: Reverse stress testing.

statement: Macroeconomic stress testing starts from a specific institutional failure and works backward to identify the circumstances that could cause it.
explanation: Macroeconomic stress testing runs forward from regulator-supplied macroeconomic shocks such as GDP, unemployment and inflation. Working backward from failure is the defining feature of reverse stress testing.
originalText: Macroeconomic stress testing.

statement: Reverse stress testing takes an institution-specific adverse outcome, such as the loss of a major client, credit rating downgrades or significant portfolio losses, as its starting point and works backward to the causes.
explanation: Reverse stress testing begins from a specific failure outcome and identifies the circumstances that could lead to it.
originalText: Reverse stress testing.

statement: Macroeconomic stress testing starts from institution-specific shocks such as the loss of a major client, credit rating downgrades and significant portfolio losses.
explanation: Macroeconomic stress testing starts from macroeconomic shocks such as changes in GDP, unemployment and inflation. Institution-specific adverse outcomes are the starting point of reverse stress testing.
originalText: Macroeconomic stress testing.

statement: Reverse stress testing starts from a specific failure outcome, such as the loss of a licence or massive cyber losses, and works backward to identify the circumstances that could cause it.
explanation: Working backward from a defined failure outcome is the defining feature of reverse stress testing.
originalText: Analyst 2 only.

statement: Macroeconomic stress testing assesses potential changes in the dependencies between measurable and immeasurable risks faced by a bank under adverse economic conditions.
explanation: Macroeconomic stress testing takes the most holistic view of risk, covering both measurable and immeasurable risks and the dependencies between them.
originalText: Assessing potential changes in dependencies between different measurable and immeasurable risks faced by the bank under adverse economic conditions.

statement: Analyzing the impact of a three-standard-deviation increase in interest rates on the modeled value of a bond portfolio is macroeconomic stress testing.
explanation: Shocking a single model input in this way is parameter (model) stress testing, which is quantitative and applies to measurable risks.
originalText: Analyzing the impact of a three‑standard‑deviation increase in interest rates on the modeled value of the bank’s bond portfolio.

statement: Determining how severe a financial market crisis would need to be to result in a bank's insolvency is macroeconomic stress testing.
explanation: This starts from a defined failure outcome and works backward, which is reverse stress testing.
originalText: Determining how severe a financial market crisis would need to be in order to result in the bank’s insolvency.

statement: A standard loss distribution approach has no risk drivers and assumes the firm's risk exposure is unchanged over time, so it cannot show how losses respond to a changing macroeconomic environment.
explanation: Stress testing aims to show how exposure changes with the macroeconomic environment, but a standard loss distribution approach treats a higher observed loss as just another draw from the same distribution.
originalText: It has no risk drivers and assumes the firm’s risk exposure is unchanged over time, so it cannot show how losses respond to a changing macroeconomic environment.

statement: A standard loss distribution approach cannot be combined with Monte Carlo simulation, so stressed losses cannot be projected.
explanation: Monte Carlo simulation of frequency and severity distributions is the core of the loss distribution approach.
originalText: It cannot be combined with Monte Carlo simulation, so stressed losses cannot be projected.

statement: A standard loss distribution approach models only loss severity, so frequency stresses cannot be reflected.
explanation: The loss distribution approach models both frequency and severity.
originalText: It models only loss severity, so frequency stresses cannot be reflected.

statement: A standard loss distribution approach is acceptable only for regulatory capital and is prohibited by regulators for stress testing.
explanation: Regulators do not prohibit the loss distribution approach for stress testing. Its real weaknesses are the lack of risk drivers and the assumption of unchanged exposure.
originalText: It is acceptable only for regulatory capital and is prohibited by regulators for stress testing.

statement: A challenge in building a conditional loss distribution approach model for stress testing is justifying the severity percentile, because the 99.9th percentile used for regulatory capital would leave the bank perpetually projected as undercapitalized.
explanation: In a conditional model, frequency is forecast from macroeconomic variables and expert judgment selects the severity percentile. The capital-standard 99.9th percentile is inappropriate for stress testing.
originalText: Justifying the percentile chosen for the severity distribution, because the 99.9th percentile used for regulatory capital would leave the bank perpetually projected as undercapitalized.

statement: In operational risk stress testing, legal losses occur in the same quarter as an adverse macroeconomic shock, so the forecast must be contemporaneous with the shock.
explanation: Legal losses lag macroeconomic events, sometimes by years, so the forecast must build in lags.
originalText: Legal losses occur in the same quarter as an adverse macroeconomic shock, so the forecast must be contemporaneous with the shock.

statement: Regulators require the 99.9th percentile to be used for severity in operational risk stress tests, which leaves no room for expert judgment.
explanation: Regulators impose no percentile requirement for stress testing, so expert judgment is needed to choose the severity percentile.
originalText: Regulators require the 99.9th percentile to be used for severity in stress tests, which leaves no room for expert judgment.

statement: A standard loss distribution approach is preferred over regression for operational risk stress testing because it has explicit macroeconomic risk drivers.
explanation: A standard loss distribution approach has no risk drivers and is considered a secondary approach. Regression-based and conditional approaches bring in macroeconomic variables.
originalText: Standard LDA is preferred over regression because it has explicit macroeconomic risk drivers.

statement: To forecast legal losses in an operational risk stress test, legal losses should be broken out into their own module, with lags built in between the macroeconomic drivers and the occurrence of the legal losses.
explanation: Litigation losses are large, and settlements can come years after a macroeconomic shock, so the forecast must model that delay.
originalText: Break legal losses out into their own module and build in lags between the macroeconomic drivers and the occurrence of the legal losses.

statement: In an operational risk stress test, legal losses should be forecast as part of total operational losses without separating them, so that they respond immediately to the macroeconomic scenario.
explanation: Legal losses should be broken out separately, and they do not respond immediately because they lag the macroeconomic event.
originalText: Forecast legal losses as part of total operational losses without separating them, so they respond immediately to the macroeconomic scenario.

statement: Legal losses should be excluded from an operational risk stress test model because they cannot be linked to the macroeconomic scenario within the stress horizon.
explanation: Legal losses are material for many banks, so excluding them understates stressed losses. They should be modelled in a separate module with lags.
originalText: Exclude legal losses from the model because they cannot be linked to the macroeconomic scenario within the stress horizon.

statement: A significant challenge in estimating the legal loss module of an operational risk stress test is that there is a lag between the macroeconomic event itself and the incurrence of legal losses.
explanation: Legal losses can materialize years after the shock, so the module must include lags between its drivers and the losses.
originalText: there is a lag between the macroeconomic event itself and the incurrence of legal losses.

statement: Future litigation cases cannot be estimated in the legal loss module of an operational risk stress test.
explanation: The legal loss module explicitly forecasts future litigation cases, as well as immaterial cases and losses above a threshold for current cases.
originalText: future litigation cases cannot be estimated.

statement: Banks are minimally impacted by legal losses in operational risk stress testing.
explanation: Litigation is a large share of operational losses for most banks.
originalText: banks are minimally impacted by legal losses.

statement: In operational risk stress testing, operational risks and legal losses cannot be separated.
explanation: Legal losses should be broken out as a separate module of the stress test.
originalText: operational risks and legal losses cannot be separated.

statement: In a comprehensive operational risk stress testing framework, risks that apply only to each unique bank are best captured in the idiosyncratic scenario add-on module.
explanation: The framework has three modules: the expected nonlegal loss forecast, the legal loss module and the idiosyncratic scenario add-on. Bank-specific vulnerabilities and storylines belong in the add-on.
originalText: Idiosyncratic scenario add‑on.

statement: In a comprehensive operational risk stress testing framework, the legal loss module is the one that best captures risks applicable only to each unique bank.
explanation: The legal loss module covers litigation losses only. Bank-specific risks are captured by the idiosyncratic scenario add-on.
originalText: Legal loss.

statement: In a comprehensive operational risk stress testing framework, the expected nonlegal loss forecast module is the one that best captures risks applicable only to each unique bank.
explanation: The expected nonlegal loss forecast projects losses by risk type from quantitative models refined by expert judgment. Bank-specific storylines belong in the idiosyncratic scenario add-on.
originalText: Expected nonlegal loss forecast.

statement: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, Singapore's guidance focuses on the early detection of cyber intrusions.
explanation: Each jurisdiction's guidance has a different emphasis. Singapore stresses early detection of intrusions.
originalText: Singapore: early detection of cyber intrusions

statement: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, Hong Kong's guidance focuses on common procedures and methodologies for the assessment of ICT risk.
explanation: Hong Kong's guidance concerns the importance of effective cyber-security risk management. Common procedures and methodologies for assessing ICT risk are the focus of the European Banking Authority.
originalText: Hong Kong: common procedures and methodologies for the assessment of ICT risk
correction: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, Hong Kong's guidance focuses on the importance of effective cyber-security risk management.

changes.from: common procedures and methodologies for the assessment of ICT risk
changes.to: the importance of effective cyber-security risk management

statement: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, Brazil's guidance focuses on the importance of effective cyber-security risk management.
explanation: Brazil's guidance concerns the establishment of a cyber security policy. The importance of effective cyber-security risk management is Hong Kong's focus.
originalText: Brazil: the importance of effective cyber‑security risk management
correction: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, Brazil's guidance focuses on the establishment of a cyber security policy.

changes.from: the importance of effective cyber-security risk management
changes.to: the establishment of a cyber security policy

statement: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, the European Banking Authority's guidance focuses on the establishment of a cyber security policy.
explanation: The EBA's guidance concerns common procedures and methodologies for assessing ICT risk. Establishing a cyber security policy is Brazil's focus.
originalText: European Banking Authority: the establishment of a cyber security policy
correction: In the Basel Committee's 2018 report on cyber-resilience practices, the European Banking Authority's guidance focuses on common procedures and methodologies for the assessment of ICT risk.

changes.from: the establishment of a cyber security policy
changes.to: common procedures and methodologies for the assessment of ICT risk

statement: The FSB Lexicon definition of cyber-resilience means eliminating all cyber vulnerabilities so that incidents cannot occur.
explanation: Cyber-resilience is the ability to continue to carry out the organisation's mission by anticipating and adapting to threats and by withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from incidents. It accepts that incidents will occur.
originalText: Eliminating all cyber vulnerabilities so that incidents cannot occur

statement: Under the FSB Lexicon definition, cyber-resilience includes anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment.
explanation: Anticipating and adapting is one element of the definition, alongside withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from incidents.
originalText: Anticipating and adapting to cyber threats and other relevant changes in the environment

statement: Under the FSB Lexicon definition, cyber-resilience includes withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from cyber incidents.
explanation: This is the second element of the definition, alongside anticipating and adapting to threats.
originalText: Withstanding, containing and rapidly recovering from cyber incidents

statement: Under the FSB Lexicon definition, cyber-resilience is the ability of an organisation to continue to carry out its mission.
explanation: Continuing the mission is the core of the definition.
originalText: Continuing to carry out the organisation’s mission

statement: According to the Basel Committee, greater use of automation, third-party service providers and cloud services grows the attack surface, enlarges the perimeter of interest to regulators, and with cloud services makes that perimeter shared.
explanation: More automation and integration produce an attack surface accessible from anywhere. Third-party use enlarges the regulatory perimeter, and a shared perimeter means institutions must build resilience in partnership with providers.
originalText: The attack surface grows and is accessible from anywhere, the perimeter of interest to regulators becomes bigger with third‑party use, and cloud services make that perimeter shared

statement: According to the Basel Committee, outsourcing data processing to third parties shrinks the regulators' perimeter of interest because the data are held outside the institution.
explanation: Third-party use enlarges, not shrinks, the perimeter of interest to regulators.
originalText: Outsourcing data processing to third parties shrinks the regulators’ perimeter of interest because data is held outside the institution

statement: According to the Basel Committee, cloud services make the perimeter the sole responsibility of the cloud provider, so the bank's own cyber-resilience duties fall away.
explanation: The perimeter becomes shared, not transferred. The institution must still build and maintain its own cyber-resilience in partnership with the provider.
originalText: Cloud services make the perimeter the sole responsibility of the cloud provider, so the bank’s own cyber‑resilience duties fall away

statement: According to the Basel Committee, greater automation reduces the attack surface, which lowers the incentive for cyber-adversaries to increase their capabilities.
explanation: Greater automation and integration enlarge the attack surface, which gives adversaries more incentive to increase their capabilities.
originalText: Greater automation reduces the attack surface, which lowers the incentive for cyber‑adversaries to increase their capabilities

statement: Sharing of cybersecurity information among regulators is the least commonly observed type of information sharing across jurisdictions.
explanation: Sharing among regulators is typically ad hoc, bilateral or within supervisory colleges, with less systematic arrangements.
originalText: Sharing among regulators

statement: Sharing of cybersecurity information among banks is the least commonly observed type of information sharing across jurisdictions.
explanation: Sharing among banks is one of the three most commonly observed types, together with sharing by banks and regulators with security agencies and sharing from banks to regulators.
originalText: Sharing among banks

statement: Sharing of cybersecurity information by banks and regulators with security agencies is the least commonly observed type of information sharing across jurisdictions.
explanation: Sharing with security agencies is one of the three most commonly observed types. Sharing among regulators is the least observed.
originalText: Sharing by banks and regulators with security agencies

statement: The scope and depth of cybersecurity information sharing among banks may vary significantly between financial markets, depending on the level of trust among participating banks.
explanation: Sharing among banks relies on trust and industry culture, so it often starts within a small group before widening.
originalText: The scope and depth of information‑sharing practices among banks may significantly vary between financial markets, depending on the level of trust among participating banks.

statement: Sharing of cybersecurity information among banks is less frequently observed and generally considered less effective than other cybersecurity information-sharing practices.
explanation: Sharing among banks is one of the three most commonly observed types of cybersecurity information sharing.
originalText: The sharing of cybersecurity information among banks is less frequently observed and generally considered to be less effective than other cyber‑security information‑sharing practices.

statement: Information sharing among different national regulators has evolved significantly over the past several years and is now a widespread practice in a large majority of jurisdictions.
explanation: Sharing among regulators is the least observed type and remains largely ad hoc.
originalText: Information‑sharing among different national regulators has evolved significantly over the past several years and is now a widespread practice at a large majority of jurisdictions.

statement: Existing peer-sharing mechanisms among banks focus on exchanging information on cyber-security incidents, but such information is generally not shared from banks to regulators.
explanation: Banks do share incident information with regulators, frequently because it is mandated. Peer sharing mainly concerns threat information.
originalText: Existing peer‑sharing mechanisms among banks focus on the exchange of information related to cyber‑security incidents, but such information is generally not shared from banks to regulators.

statement: In jurisdictions where information sharing among banks is already well established, sharing of cybersecurity information from regulators to banks tends to be less prevalent.
explanation: Where banks have a well-functioning mechanism to share among themselves, they have less need for cyber information from regulators.
originalText: Sharing from regulators to banks

statement: In jurisdictions where information sharing among banks is already well established, sharing of cybersecurity information from banks to regulators tends to be less prevalent.
explanation: Bank-to-regulator reporting is usually mandated and is not displaced by peer sharing among banks.
originalText: Sharing from banks to regulators

statement: A stress test modeler must consider capital actions such as acquisitions, spin-offs, dividend changes and share repurchases or issuance, because they deplete or conserve capital.
explanation: Each quarter the modeler must make assumptions about these actions, which makes projecting the balance sheet over the horizon difficult.
originalText: Greta and Dace only.

statement: Balance sheet modeling for a stress test is difficult only if a dynamic balance sheet is assumed; under a static balance sheet the modeler need not consider capital actions.
explanation: The difficulty of modeling the balance sheet and capital actions exists under both static and dynamic balance sheet assumptions.
originalText: John only.

statement: Regardless of whether the denominator of the capital ratio is common equity or risk-weighted assets, determining post-stress capital adequacy requires modeling both the income statement and the balance sheet over the stress test horizon, which is typically about two years.
explanation: Post-stress capital ratios depend on the evolution of both flows (income) and stocks (balance sheet) over the horizon.
originalText: Regardless of whether the denominator in the capital ratio is common equity or risk‑weighted assets (RWA), determining post‑stress capital adequacy requires modeling both the income statement and the balance sheet over the course of the stress test horizon, which is typically about two years

statement: Compared to the banking book, stress testing the trading book is more difficult because it is a newer discipline.
explanation: Formal stress testing of the banking book, dominated by credit risk, is the newer discipline, and implementing stress scenarios in the trading book is more straightforward.
originalText: Compared to the banking book, stress testing the trading book is more difficult because it is a newer discipline

statement: Implementing stress scenarios for revenues is much more developed and easier than stress testing for losses.
explanation: Revenue modeling is far less developed and harder than loss modeling.
originalText: Implementing stress scenarios for revenues is much more developed and easier than stress testing for losses

statement: The most robust stress tests assume loss severity rates (loss given default) that are invariant to geography, business cycle or industry and uniformly represent worst-case scenarios.
explanation: Loss given default varies with geography, the business cycle and industry. One-size-fits-all severities make the mapping from macro factors to bank results less meaningful.
originalText: The most robust stress tests assume loss severity (i.e., loss given default, LGD) rates that are invariant to geography, business cycle, or industry and uniformly represent the worst‑case scenarios

statement: Credit card loan losses are especially sensitive to unemployment rates, so regional differences in unemployment produce very different card loss rates.
explanation: This is why macro-variable stress tests can mislead for banks exposed to different geographies, as shown by the wide range of US state unemployment rates after the 2007-2009 crisis.
originalText: Credit card loans.

statement: Assumptions about acquisitions and spin-offs, dividend changes, and share buybacks or issuance make it especially challenging to model a bank's balance sheet over a stress test horizon.
explanation: These capital actions change both capital and assets each quarter, so the balance sheet path requires many judgment-based assumptions.
originalText: model a bank’s balance sheet over a stress test horizon.

statement: In modeling bank revenues over a stress test horizon, total income is split into interest and noninterest income, and noninterest income (fees, service charges) is especially hard to model even though its share of bank income has been rising.
explanation: Noninterest income is increasingly important but the hardest part of revenue to model.
originalText: Total income is split into interest and noninterest income; noninterest income (fees, service charges) is especially hard to model, even though its share of bank income has been rising.

statement: Revenue modeling is more developed than loss modeling because the 2009 SCAP specified a detailed revenue methodology.
explanation: The SCAP gave little guidance on revenue, and revenue modeling remains much less developed than loss modeling.

statement: Interest income is easy to model for stress testing because the yield curve fully determines how changing rates affect bank profitability.
explanation: The yield curve helps estimate interest income, but how rate changes affect overall profitability remains unclear.
originalText: Interest income is easy to model because the yield curve fully determines how changing rates affect bank profitability.

statement: Noninterest income can be ignored in stress testing because it is a small and declining share of US bank income.
explanation: The share of noninterest income in bank income has been steadily increasing, so ignoring it would be a serious omission.
originalText: Noninterest income can be ignored because it is a small and declining share of U.S. bank income.

statement: In the RAROC measure, the numerator is after-tax expected risk-adjusted net income and the denominator is economic capital.
explanation: RAROC divides after-tax expected income, net of expected losses, by economic capital, which proxies for risk.
originalText: The numerator is after‑tax expected risk‑adjusted net income and the denominator is economic capital.

statement: The numerator of RAROC is pretax risk-adjusted net income.
explanation: Taxes are deducted in the numerator, so RAROC uses after-tax expected risk-adjusted net income.
originalText: The numerator is pretax risk‑adjusted net income.
correction: The numerator of RAROC is after-tax risk-adjusted net income.

statement: Regulatory capital is the denominator of RAROC.
explanation: The denominator of RAROC is economic capital, a proxy for risk, rather than the rule-based regulatory capital amount.
originalText: Regulatory capital is the denominator.
correction: Economic capital is the denominator of RAROC.

statement: In the RAROC numerator, expected losses are set to zero when the activity is a credit exposure.
explanation: For credit exposures, expected default losses are the main expected loss deducted from the numerator.
originalText: Expected losses are set to zero in the numerator when the activity is a credit exposure.

statement: In the RAROC formula, the denominator is economic capital, the buffer held against unexpected losses at the bank's chosen confidence level, which serves as the proxy for risk.
explanation: The numerator measures reward and the denominator measures risk, which captures the risk-reward trade-off.
originalText: Economic capital, the buffer held against unexpected losses at the bank’s chosen confidence level, which serves as the proxy for risk.

statement: In the RAROC formula, the denominator is the loan amount, which proxies for the revenue the loan can generate.
explanation: The denominator is economic capital, which measures risk. The loan amount is not the denominator.
originalText: The loan amount, which proxies for the revenue the loan can generate.

statement: In the RAROC formula, the denominator is the bank's cost of capital, used as the benchmark that the loan's return must exceed.
explanation: The cost of equity or hurdle rate is the benchmark that RAROC is compared with. It is not the denominator.
originalText: The bank’s cost of capital, used as the benchmark that the loan’s return must exceed.

statement: Net present value is incompatible with the CAPM and has no convenient way of incorporating risk.
explanation: NPV is built on the CAPM and incorporates risk through a risk-adjusted discount rate based on beta.
originalText: NPV is incompatible with the CAPM and has no convenient way of incorporating risk.
correction: Net present value uses a CAPM-based risk-adjusted discount rate to incorporate risk.

changes.from: is incompatible with the CAPM and has no convenient way of incorporating risk
changes.to: uses a CAPM-based risk-adjusted discount rate to incorporate risk

statement: RAROC adjusts the numerator by deducting expected loss from the return and adjusts the denominator by substituting economic capital for accounting capital.
explanation: These are the two adjustments that turn a simple return on capital measure into RAROC.

statement: Return on equity and return on assets rely on accounting book values and therefore do not capture the underlying risk.
explanation: Accounting measures ignore risk, which is the gap that RAROC is designed to fill.

statement: RAROC can be used for capital allocation on an ex ante basis, using expected revenues and losses, and for performance evaluation on an ex post basis, using realized revenues and losses.
explanation: Ex ante, RAROC guides capital allocation with expected figures. Ex post, it judges performance against realized outcomes.
originalText: All four

statement: If a business unit's cost of equity is greater than its RAROC, the business unit is not adding value for shareholders.
explanation: The cost of equity is the minimum return shareholders require, so a RAROC below it means value destruction.
originalText: If a business unit’s cost of equity is greater than its RAROC, then the business unit is not adding value to shareholders.

statement: In the context of performance measurement, RAROC uses accounting profits.
explanation: RAROC is based on economic profits, with expected losses deducted and economic capital in the denominator.
correction: In the context of performance measurement, RAROC uses economic profits.

statement: In the numerator of the RAROC equation, expected loss is added to the return.
explanation: Expected loss is deducted from the return in the numerator.
correction: In the numerator of the RAROC equation, expected loss is deducted from the return.

statement: RAROC is useful for determining incentive compensation, but it lacks the flexibility to consider deferred or contingent compensation.
explanation: RAROC is flexible enough to accommodate deferred or contingent compensation and clawbacks.

statement: Choosing a lower confidence level is not likely to reduce the amount of risk capital required if the firm has little exposure to operational, credit and settlement risks.
explanation: A lower confidence level cuts risk capital sharply mainly for firms dominated by risks with rare, very large losses, such as operational, credit and settlement risks.
originalText: II only.

statement: Selecting a longer time horizon for RAROC calculations is preferable because risk and return data are more reliable with more time.
explanation: Practitioners use a one-year horizon, reflecting the business planning cycle and time to recapitalize. Risk and return data beyond one year are of low quality.
originalText: I only.

statement: A through-the-cycle (TTC) approach to default probabilities is more likely to result in lower volatility of capital than a point-in-time (PIT) approach.
explanation: TTC probabilities smooth the economic cycle, so ratings and economic capital are more stable than under PIT.
originalText: A TTC approach is more likely to result in a lower volatility of capital compared to the PIT approach.

statement: A through-the-cycle (TTC) approach should be used to price financial instruments with credit risk exposure.
explanation: Pricing credit-risk instruments uses the point-in-time approach, which reflects current conditions.
originalText: A through‑the‑cycle (TTC) approach should be used to price financial instruments with credit risk exposure.
correction: A point-in-time (PIT) approach should be used to price financial instruments with credit risk exposure.

statement: A point-in-time (PIT) approach is more commonly used for computations involving profitability and strategic decisions.
explanation: The through-the-cycle approach is more commonly used for economic capital, profitability and strategic decisions.
originalText: A point‑in‑time (PIT) approach is more commonly used for computations involving profitability and strategic decisions.
correction: A through-the-cycle (TTC) approach is more commonly used for computations involving profitability and strategic decisions.

statement: A firm's rating will not change when analyzed under the point-in-time approach versus the through-the-cycle approach.
explanation: Ratings are more likely to change under PIT than under TTC, because PIT responds to current conditions.
originalText: A firm’s rating will not change when analyzed under the PIT approach versus the TTC approach.

statement: Large diversification benefits can arise when operational risk is aggregated with other risks.
explanation: Operational risk is relatively weakly correlated with market and credit risk, so the aggregate capital is well below the simple sum.

statement: Diversification can be achieved only across different risk classes, never within one risk class.
explanation: Diversification benefits also arise across business lines and activities within a single risk type.

statement: The diversification benefit of the firm can be allocated back to business units in an objective way, with no subjectivity.
explanation: Allocating the diversification benefit to units is highly subjective and affects their performance measures.

statement: A diversification benefit exists whenever the correlation between two risks is exactly +1.
explanation: At a correlation of +1 the aggregate equals the simple sum, so there is no diversification benefit.
correction: A diversification benefit exists whenever the correlation between two risks is below +1.

statement: Fully diversified capital should be used to assess the firm's solvency and minimum risk pricing.
explanation: Fully diversified capital allocates the whole diversification benefit, so the allocations add up to the firm's total risk capital.
originalText: Fully diversified capital (\$56 for X and \$64 for Y) should be used to assess the firm’s solvency and minimum risk pricing.

statement: Incremental (marginal) capital should be used for active portfolio management and business mix decisions.
explanation: Marginal capital fully reflects diversification effects, so it suits decisions on adding or removing activities.
originalText: Incremental capital (\$40 for X and \$50 for Y) should be used for active portfolio management and business mix decisions.

statement: Stand-alone capital can be used for incentive compensation, while fully diversified capital can be used to assess the extra performance generated by diversification.
explanation: These are the standard uses of the stand-alone and fully diversified capital measures.
originalText: Stand‑alone capital can be used for incentive compensation, while fully diversified capital can be used to assess the extra performance generated by diversification.

statement: When business units complain that a RAROC system attributes too much economic capital to them, senior management should display commitment to RAROC and expand in-house communication and education about the system.
explanation: Best practice pairs visible top-management commitment with transparent communication and education so that capital allocation is seen as fair.
originalText: Display commitment to RAROC, expand in‑house communication and education regarding the system.

statement: When business units are dissatisfied with a RAROC system, senior management should neglect the dissatisfaction and enforce the system at all costs.
explanation: Ignoring concerns breeds resistance. Best practice calls for open dialogue, communication and education.
originalText: Neglect dissatisfaction in the local management and enforce the RAROC system at all costs.

statement: Implementing a RAROC system tends to decrease the frequency of risk parameter reviews.
explanation: Economic capital depends on risk parameters such as PD, LGD, volatility and correlation, so these must be reviewed more, not less, frequently.
originalText: Decrease in the frequency of risk parameter reviews
correction: Implementing a RAROC system tends to increase the frequency of risk parameter reviews.

statement: Implementing a RAROC system tends to increase disputes over economic capital allocations.
explanation: Explicit economic capital charges make business units challenge the fairness of their allocations.
originalText: Increase in disputes over economic capital allocations

statement: Implementing a RAROC system tends to cause resources to be reallocated from lower-RAROC units to higher-RAROC units.
explanation: RAROC works like an internal capital market that directs scarce resources toward higher-RAROC units.
originalText: Reallocation of resources from lower to higher RAROC units

statement: Implementing a RAROC system tends to increase activity in the parameter review group.
explanation: Because economic capital is sensitive to the parameters, the review group becomes more important.
originalText: Increased activity in the parameter review group

statement: Best practice in implementing RAROC calls for an exclusively quantitative decision rule under which the firm exits any activity whose ex-ante RAROC does not exceed the hurdle rate.
explanation: Best practice combines RAROC, the quantity of earnings, with qualitative quality-of-earnings factors. An exclusively quantitative exit rule ignores strategic value.
originalText: In order to preserve the integrity and transparency of the RAROC system, there should be an exclusively quantitative decision rule for activities: if the ex‑ante RAROC does not exceed the firm’s hurdle rate (if the RAROC return is ”low”), the firm should exit the activity

statement: In implementing a RAROC system, the instructions must come from top management, and the CEO and executive team should sponsor the implementation and be active in its diffusion.
explanation: RAROC steers strategic decisions, so senior management commitment is the first recommendation for implementation.
originalText: Given the strategic nature of the decisions steered by a RAROC system, the marching orders must come from the top management of the firm; specifically, the CEO and his or her executive team should sponsor the implementation of a RAROC system and should be active in its diffusion

statement: The value at risk methodologies for measuring market risk and credit risk that underpin RAROC calculations are generally well accepted by business units, although this is not yet true for operational risk; disagreements in practice concern the parameters that determine the size of economic capital.
explanation: Market and credit risk methods are comparatively accepted, while operational risk measurement is less established.
originalText: The value at risk (VaR) methodologies for measuring market risk and credit risk that underpin RAROC calculations are ”generally well‑accepted” by business units (although this is not yet true for operational risk); in practice, disagreements concern the setting of the parameters that feed into these models which determine the size of economic capital

statement: Balance sheet requests from business units, such as economic capital, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios and risk-weighted assets, should be channeled to the RAROC group every quarter, after which limits are set for these measures.
explanation: This quarterly process is part of active capital management within a RAROC system.
originalText: Balance sheet requests from the business units, such as economic capital, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios, and risk‑weighted assets, should be channeled to the RAROC group every quarter; limits are then set for economic capital, leverage ratio, liquidity ratios, and risk‑weighted assets

statement: A restriction on the firm's growth due to leverage limitations may result in higher profits.
explanation: Leverage limits force the firm to allocate scarce capital to its best risk-adjusted uses, which can raise profitability.
originalText: A restriction on the firm’s growth due to leverage limitations may result in higher profits.

statement: A successful RAROC approach focuses on maximizing the profits earned by the firm.
explanation: RAROC focuses on how well the firm is compensated for the risks taken, not on the amount of income generated.
originalText: A successful RAROC approach is focused on maximizing profits earned by the firm.

statement: In a RAROC approach, data collection throughout the firm should be decentralized so that business units can ensure the utmost accuracy of data.
explanation: Data collection should be centralized with edit and reasonability checks. The RAROC group is accountable for it, and units are accountable only for the data they produce.
originalText: The data collection process throughout the firm should be decentralized to allow the various business units to ensure the utmost accuracy of data.

statement: Metrics involving credit risk, market risk and operational risk used to compute economic capital are generally clearly defined and may be computed objectively.
explanation: Credit and market risk metrics are comparatively well defined, but operational risk metrics involve significant subjectivity and debate.
originalText: Metrics involving credit risk, market risk, and operational risk to compute economic capital are generally clearly defined and may be computed objectively.

statement: All major copulas automatically ensure that Pearson linear correlation accurately describes the true dependence structure, even when dependence is dynamic.
explanation: Linear correlation is not the only dependence measure, and a copula does not guarantee a correct or time-varying dependence structure. Its parameters still have to be estimated and validated.
originalText: Pearson linear correlation is the only dependence input available, but all major copulas automatically ensure it accurately describes the true dependence structure even when dependence is dynamic.

statement: The copula approach allows simulation of the entire distribution of aggregate losses, not only the tails.
explanation: Simulating from the copula gives the whole aggregate loss distribution.

statement: Given the same marginal distributions, different copula functions can be simulated to see the effect of the assumed dependence structure.
explanation: A copula separates the marginal distributions from the dependence structure, so copulas such as the Gaussian and t can be swapped as a sensitivity test.
originalText: Given the same marginal distributions, she can test (simulate) different copula functions to see the effect of the assumed dependence structure.

statement: A copula places no requirement on the form of the marginal distributions it joins, so the marginals may be skewed or heavy-tailed.
explanation: Because the dependence structure is modeled separately, the marginals can take any form.
originalText: The marginals may be skewed or heavy‑tailed, because a copula places no requirement on the form of the univariate distributions it joins.

statement: Economic capital is most often parameterized as the capital a bank needs to absorb unexpected losses over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level.
explanation: Expected losses are covered by pricing and provisioning, so capital is needed only for unexpected losses.
originalText: Capital a bank needs to absorb unexpected losses (UL) over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level

statement: Economic capital is most often parameterized as the capital a bank needs to absorb expected losses over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level.
explanation: Expected losses are covered by pricing and provisions. Economic capital is held against unexpected losses.
originalText: Capital a bank needs to absorb expected losses (EL) over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level

statement: Economic capital is most often parameterized as the capital a bank needs to absorb both expected and unexpected losses over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level.
explanation: Adding expected losses would double count what pricing and provisions already cover.
originalText: Capital a bank needs to absorb both expected losses (EL) and unexpected losses (UL) over a certain time horizon at a given confidence level

statement: According to the BIS, the three common credit models tend to produce significantly different economic capital estimates in both default-only mode and mark-to-market mode.
explanation: The IACPM and ISDA study found large differences in economic capital estimates across the models.
originalText: I, II and III

statement: In a severe recession, point-in-time default probabilities rise sharply while through-the-cycle probabilities change little, so economic capital based on through-the-cycle probabilities understates near-term default risk relative to a point-in-time view.
explanation: PIT probabilities respond to current conditions, whereas TTC probabilities are averaged across the cycle and are relatively stable.
originalText: PIT default probabilities will rise sharply, while TTC probabilities will change little, so TTC‑based economic capital understates near‑term default risk relative to a PIT view.

statement: In a severe recession, through-the-cycle default probabilities rise sharply while point-in-time probabilities change little.
explanation: The definitions are reversed. Point-in-time probabilities are cyclical and rise quickly in a downturn, while through-the-cycle probabilities are smoothed.
originalText: TTC default probabilities will rise sharply, while PIT probabilities will change little, so PIT‑based measures understate near‑term default risk.

statement: Point-in-time and through-the-cycle default probabilities must be identical because both use the same time horizon.
explanation: A common horizon does not make them equal. They differ in how cyclical conditions enter the estimate.
originalText: PIT and TTC default probabilities must be identical because both use the same time horizon.

statement: According to the BIS survey, banks most commonly assume a high correlation between market and credit risk, a lower correlation between business risk and credit or market risk, and a very low correlation between operational risk and all other risks.
explanation: Operational risk is therefore assumed to have the lowest correlation with other risks, which produces large diversification benefits in aggregation.
originalText: III, II, I

statement: The BIS asserts that validation of economic capital models is a quantitative process by definition, but not a qualitative process.
explanation: The BIS stresses that validation combines qualitative and quantitative elements.
originalText: Validation is a quantitative process by definition, but it is NOT a qualitative process
correction: The BIS asserts that validation of economic capital models combines qualitative and quantitative elements.

changes.from: is a quantitative process by definition, but not a qualitative process

statement: The BIS defines validation of internal economic capital models broadly as all processes that provide evidence-based assessments of a model's fitness for its purpose, both before deployment (ex ante) and afterward through ex-post statistical tests.
explanation: Validation is not limited to statistical back-testing after the model is in use.
originalText: Validation refers broadly to all processes that provide evidence‑based assessments about a model’s fitness for its purpose, including both ”before deployment” (ex‑ante) and afterward as ex‑post statistical tests

statement: Benchmarking is a common and useful validation process, but its drawback is that it does not test a model against reality.
explanation: Benchmarking compares one model with another, so it gives no direct evidence about how the model performs against actual outcomes.
originalText: Benchmarking is a common and useful validation process, but its drawback is that it does not test against reality

statement: The BIS notes that a wide range of validation techniques makes a layered approach possible, and that generally the more layers, the better.
explanation: Each additional layer gives more evidence about the model's performance.
originalText: There are a wide range of validation techniques making possible a ”layered approach,” and generally, the more layers, the better

statement: According to the BIS, correlation estimates from current economic capital models are inaccurate and unstable mainly because they depend heavily on explicit or implicit model assumptions.
explanation: Assumptions such as stable correlations or a Gaussian copula may fail, especially in stress, which makes the estimates fragile.
originalText: depend heavily on explicit or implicit model assumptions

statement: Correlation estimates cannot be incorporated into any risk aggregation approach.
explanation: Correlations are routinely used in aggregation, for example in the variance-covariance approach.
originalText: cannot be incorporated into any aggregation approach

statement: Correlations used in economic capital models are fixed by supervisors rather than estimated by the bank.
explanation: Banks estimate or assume the correlations themselves.
originalText: are fixed by supervisors rather than estimated by the bank

statement: Bonds with embedded options pose a greater challenge to the determination of a bank's economic capital than ordinary stocks, preference shares or plain fixed-rate loans, because embedded optionality makes cash flows uncertain and payoffs nonlinear.
explanation: Exercise of the options depends on borrower behavior and future rates, so a simple linear sensitivity measure understates the risk.
originalText: Bonds with embedded options.

statement: Capturing wrong-way risk in economic capital for counterparty credit risk is difficult because it requires understanding the counterparty's often opaque market risk factor sensitivities and comparing them with the bank's own exposures, and because its magnitude is hard to quantify over a one-year horizon at a high confidence level.
explanation: Wrong-way risk arises when exposure to a counterparty rises at the same time as its credit quality deteriorates.
originalText: Identifying it requires understanding the counterparty’s market risk factor sensitivities (often opaque, e.g., a hedge fund) and comparing them with the bank’s own exposures, and its magnitude is hard to quantify over a one‑year horizon at a high confidence level.

statement: Exposure at default and PD/LGD are always estimated jointly in economic capital models, so the wrong-way risk interaction is double counted.
explanation: Exposure and PD/LGD are frequently estimated separately, which is why the interaction between them is missed rather than double counted.
originalText: Exposure at default and PD/LGD are always estimated jointly, so the interaction is double counted.

statement: Regulators do not permit wrong-way risk to be reflected in economic capital.
explanation: Wrong-way risk may be incorporated in economic capital, for example through an add-on.
originalText: Regulators do not permit wrong‑way risk to be reflected in economic capital.

statement: In counterparty credit risk, exposure and counterparty creditworthiness are statistically independent, so there is no relationship to model for wrong-way risk.
explanation: Wrong-way risk is defined by the dependence between exposure and counterparty credit quality, so assuming independence ignores it.
originalText: Exposure and counterparty creditworthiness are statistically independent, so there is no relationship to model.

statement: The main challenge in choosing a risk measure for economic capital purposes is that there is no singularly preferred risk measure.
explanation: Standard deviation, VaR, expected shortfall and spectral measures each have advantages and disadvantages, so the choice must fit the intended application.
originalText: There is no singularly preferred risk measure for economic capital purposes.

statement: The main challenge in choosing a risk measure for economic capital purposes is that there are no generally accepted properties of a good risk measure.
explanation: There is general agreement on desirable properties, such as being intuitive, stable, easy to compute and coherent. The difficulty is that no measure satisfies all of them.
originalText: There are no generally accepted properties of a good risk measure.

statement: Combining economic capital components that were calculated at different confidence levels and time horizons, without first expressing them on a common basis, makes the aggregate figure inaccurate.
explanation: Aggregation requires comparable units, meaning the same risk metric, confidence level and time horizon.
originalText: Combining component measures that were calculated at different confidence levels and time horizons without first expressing them on a common basis.
